name: Rufinus
bio: Rufinus wrote some of the most polished erotic epigrams in the Anthology. Nothing certain is known of him, and his date is uncertain, perhaps the second to the fourth century AD.

Paton's index lists a Rufinus Domesticus separately; the epigrams under that name are not filed here. The poems here are all those Paton heads “Rufinus” or attributes to him as “by the same”, mostly in Book V.

poems.title: Book V, 9: Written from Ephesus in the form of a letter
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I, thy Rufinus, wish all joy to my sweetest Elpis, if she can have joy away from me. By thy eyes, can support no longer this desolate separation and my lonely bed without thee. Ever bathed in tears I go to Coressus hill or to the temple of Artemis the Great. But to-morrow my own city shall receive me back and I shall fly to the light of thy eyes wishing thee a thousand blessings.

poems.title: Book V, 12
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Let us bathe, Prodike, and crown our heads, and quaff untempered wine, lifting up greater cups. Short is the season of rejoicing, and then old age comes to forbid it any longer, and at the last death.

poems.title: Book V, 14
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Europa’s kiss is sweet though it reach only to the lips, though it but lightly touch the mouth. But she touches not with the edge of the lips; with her mouth cleaving close she drains the soul from the finger-tips.

poems.title: Book V, 15
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Where is now Praxiteles ? Where are the hands of Polycleitus, that gave life to the works of ancient art ? Who shall mould Melite’s scented ringlets, or her fiery eyes and the splendour of her neck? Where are the modellers, the carvers in stone ? Such beauty, like the image of a god, deserved a temple.

poems.title: Book V, 18
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: We, who take no pleasure in costly intrigues, prefer servants to ladies of high station. The latter smell of scent, and give themselves the airs of their class, and they are attended even at the rendezvous (). The charm and fragrance of a servant are her own, and her bed is always ready without any prodigal display. I imitate Pyrrhus the son of Achilles, who preferred Andromache the slave to his wife Hermione.

poems.title: Book V, 19
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I am not said to rave about boys as before, but now they say I am mad about women, and my quoit has become a rattle. Instead of the unadulterated complexion of boys I am now fond of powder and rouge and colours that are laid on. Dolphins shall feed in the forests of Erymanthus, and fleet deer in the grey sea.

poems.title: Book V, 21
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Did I not tell thee, Prodike, that we are growing old, did I not foretell that the dissolvers of love shall come soon? Now they are here, the wrinkles and the grey hairs, a shrivelled body, and a mouth lacking all its former charm. Does anyone approach thee now, thou haughty beauty, or flatter and beseech thee? No! like a wayside tomb we now pass thee by.

poems.title: Book V, 22
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Love, the giver of sweet gifts, gave me to thee, Boépis, for a servant, yoking the steer that came himself to bend his neck to Desire, all of his own free will, at his own bidding, an abject slave who will never ask for bitter freedom, never, my dear, till he grows grey and old. May no evil eye ever look on our hopes to blight them !

poems.title: Book V, 27
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Where, Melissa, now is the golden and admired brilliance of thy renowned beauty? Where are they, thy disdainful brow and thy proud spirit, thy long slender neck, and the rich gold clasps of thy haughty ankles? Now thy hair is unadorned and unkempt and rags hang about thy feet. Such is the end of prodigal harlots.

poems.title: Book V, 28
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Now, you so chary of your favours, you bid me good-day, when the more than marble smoothness of your cheeks is gone; now you dally with me, when you have done away with the ringlets that tossed on your haughty neck. Come not near me, meet me not, scorner! I don’t accept a bramble for a rose.

poems.title: Book V, 35
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I judged the hinder charms of three; for they themselves chose me, showing me the naked splendour of their limbs. Et prima quidem signata suleculis rotundis candido florebat et molli decore ; alterius vero divaricatae nivea caro rubescebat purpurea rosa rubicundior ; tertia velut mare tranquillum sulcabatur fluctibus mutis, delicata eius cute sponte palpitante. If Paris who judged the goddesses had seen three such, he would not have wished to look again on the former ones. :

poems.title: Book V, 36
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Rhodope, Melita, and Rhodoclea strove with each other, quaenam habeat potiorem Merionem, and chose me as judge, and like those goddesses famous for their beauty, stood naked, dipped in nectar. Et Rhodopes quidem inter femora fulgebat Polyphemus velut rosarium cano scissum amne.... Rhodocleae vero feminal vitro simile erat, udaque ejus superficies velut in templo statuae recens sculptae. But as I knew well what Paris suffered owing to his judgment, I at once gave the prize to all the three goddesses.

poems.title: Book V, 37
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Take not to your arms a woman who is too slender nor one too stout, but choose the mean between the two. The first has not enough abundance of flesh, and the second has too much. Choose neither deficiency nor excess.

poems.title: Book V, 41
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Who beat you and turned you out half-naked like this? Who had so stony a heart and no eyes to see ? Perhaps he arrived inopportunely and found you with alover. Thatis a thing that happens; all women do it, my child. But henceforth when someone is in, and he is out, bolt the outer door, lest the same thing happen to you again.

poems.title: Book V, 42
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I dislike a woman who is too facile and I dislike one who is too prudish. The one consents too quickly, the other too slowly.

poems.title: Book V, 43
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Does any man turn his girl out of doors half-dressed, just because he finds a lover with her,— just as if he had never been guilty of adultery, as if he were a Pythagorean? And, so, my dear child, you will spoil your face with crying, will you, and shiver outside the maniac’s door? Wipe your eyes and stop crying, my dear, and we'll find another who is not so good at seeing things and at beating.

poems.title: Book V, 44
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Lemnion and Kerkurion, the two whores, are always riding off the harbour of Samos. Fly, all ye youth, from Aphrodite’s corsairs; he who engages, and is sunk, is swallowed up.

poems.title: Book V, 47
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I often prayed, Thalia, to have you with me at night and satisfy my passion by fervent caresses, And, now you are close to me naked with your sweet limbs, I am all languid and drowsy. O wretched spirit, what hath befallen thee? Awake and faint not. Some day shalt thou seek in vain this supreme felicity.

poems.title: Book V, 48
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Golden are her eyes and her cheeks like crystal, and her mouth more delightful than a red rose. Her neck is of marble and her bosom polished ; her feet are whiter than silver Thetis. If here and there the thistle-down glistens amid her dark locks, I heed not the white aftermath.

poems.title: Book V, 60
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: The silver-footed maiden was bathing, letting the water fall on the golden apples of her breast, smooth like curdled milk. Her rounded buttocks, their flesh more fluid than water, rolled and tossed as she moved. Her outspread hand covered swelling Eurotas, not the whole but as much as it could.

poems.title: Book V, 61
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Playing at Condax with dark-eyed Philippa I made her laugh sweetly with all herheart. “I have thrown you’ I said “twelve, and to-morrow I will throw you another twelve or even more, as I know how.” Then when she was told she came, and laughing I said to her “I wish I had called you at night too when you were coming.”

poems.title: Book V, 62
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Time has not yet quenched your beauty, but many relics of your prime survive. Your charm has not aged, nor has the loveliness departed from your bright apples or your rose. Ah! how many hearts did that once god-like beauty burn to ashes 

poems.title: Book V, 66
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Finding Prodike happily alone, I besought her, and clasping her ambrosial knees, “Save,’ I said “a man who is nearly lost, and grant me the little breath that has not left me.’”’ When I said this, she wept, but wiped away the tears and with her tender hands gently repulsed me.

poems.title: Book V, 69
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: When Pallas and golden-sandalled Hera looked on Maeonis, they both cried out from their hearts: “We will not strip again; one decision of the shepherd is enough; it is a disgrace to be worsted twice in the contest of beauty.”

poems.title: Book V, 70
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Thou hast the beauty of Cypris, the mouth of Peitho, the form and freshness of the spring Hours, the voice of Calliope, the wisdom and virtue of Themis, the skill of Athene. With thee, my beloved, the Graces are four.

poems.title: Book V, 73
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Ye gods! I knew not that Cytherea was bathing, releasing with her hands her hair to fall upon her neck. Have mercy on me, my queen, and be not wrath with my eyes that have looked on thy immortal form. Now I see! It is Rhodoclea and not Cypris. Then whence this beauty ! Thou, it would seem, hast despoiled the goddess.

poems.title: Book V, 74
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I senp thee this garland, Rhodoclea, that with my own hands I wove out of beautiful flowers. There are lilies and roses and dewy anemones, and tender narcissus and purple-gleaming violets. Wear it and cease to be vain. Both thou and the garland flower and fade.

poems.title: Book V, 75
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Know Aphrodite that Amymone, a young girl, was my neighbour and set my heart on fire not a little. She herself would jest with me, and whenever I had the opportunity I grew venturesome. She used to blush. Well! that did not help matters ; she felt the pang. With great pains I succeeded ; I am told now that she is with child. So what am I to do, be off or remain ?

poems.title: Book V, 76
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Once her complexion was lovely, her breasts like the spring-tide; all were good, her ankles, her height, her forehead, her hair. But time and old age and grey locks have wrought a change and now she is not the shadow of her former self, but wears false hair and has a wrinkled face, uglier even than an old monkey’s.

poems.title: Book V, 77
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: It women had as much charm when all is over as before, men would never tire of intercourse with their wives, but all women are displeasing then.

poems.title: Book V, 87
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Me isstas denies she is in love, but her body cries aloud that it has received a whole quiverful of arrows. Unsteady is her step and she takes her breath in snatches, and there are dark purple hollows under her eyes. But, ye Loves, by your mother, fair-wreathed Cytherea, burn the rebellious maid, till she cry, “I am burning!”

poems.title: Book V, 88
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Linkman Love, if thou canst not set two equally alight, put out or transfer the flame that burns in one.

poems.title: Book V, 92
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Rhodope is exalted by her beauty, and if I chance to say “Good day,’ salutes me only with her proud eyebrows. If I ever hang garlands over her door, she crushes them under her haughty heels in her wrath. Come quicker, wrinkles and pitiless old age; make haste. Do you at least unbend Rhodope.

poems.title: Book V, 93
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: I nave armed my breast with wisdom against Love ; nor will he conquer, if it be a single combat. I, a mortal, will stand up against an immortal. But if he has Bacchus to help him, what can I alone against two?

poems.title: Book V, 94
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Thou hast Hera’s eyes, Melite, and Athene’s hands, the breasts of Aphrodite, and the feet of Thetis. Blessed is he who looks on thee, thrice blessed he who hears thee talk, a demigod he who kisses thee, and a god he who takes thee to wife.

poems.title: Book V, 97
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: Love, if thou aimest thy bow at both of us impartially thou art a god, but if thou favourest one, no god art thou.

poems.title: Book V, 103
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text: For how long, Prodice, shall I weep at thy door? Till when shall thy hard heart be deaf to my prayers ? Already the grey hairs begin to invade thee, and soon thou shalt give thyself to me as Hecuba to Priam.

poems.title: Love and Wine (Mackail)
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I am armed against Love with a breastplate of Reason, neither shall he conquer me, one against one; yes, I a mortal will contend with him the immortal: but if he have Bacchus to second him, what can I do alone against the two?

poems.title: The Love Letter (Mackail)
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Rufinus to Elpis, my most sweet: well and very well be with her, if she can be well away from me. No longer can I bear, no, by thine eyes, my solitary and unmated severance from thee, but evermore blotted with tears I go to Coressus or to the temple of the great Artemis; but tomorrow my home shall receive me, and I will fly to thy face and bid thee a thousand greetings.

poems.title: The Maiden's Posy (Mackail)
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I send thee, Rhodocleia, this garland, which myself have twined of fair flowers beneath my hands; here is lily and rose-chalice and moist anemone, and soft narcissus and dark-glowing violet; garlanding thyself with these, cease to be high-minded; even as the garland thou also dost flower and fall.

poems.title: The Joy of Youth (Mackail)
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Let us bathe, Prodice, and garland ourselves, and drain unmixed wine, lifting larger cups; little is our life of gladness, then old age will stop the rest, and death is the end.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.9: Ῥουφῖνος τῇ μῇ γλυκερωτάτῃ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
Ῥουφῖνος τῇ μῇ γλυκερωτάτῃ Ἐλπίδι πολλὰ
χαίρειν, εἰ χαίρειν χωρὶς ἐμοῦ δύναται.
οὐκέτι βαστάζω, μὰ τὰ σ’ ὄμματα, τὴν φιλέρημον
καὶ τὴν μουνολεχῆ σεῖο διαζυγίην
ἀλλʼ αἰεὶ δακρύοισι πεφυρμένος ἢ πὶ Κορησσὸν
ἔρχομαι ἢ μεγάλης νηὸν ἐς Ἀρτέμιδος.
αὔριον ἀλλὰ πάτρη με δεδέξεται· ἐς δὲ σὸν ὄμμα
πτήσομαι, ἐρρῶσθαι μυρία σ’ εὐχόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.12: λουσάμενοι, Προδίκη, πυκασώμεθα, καὶ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
λουσάμενοι, Προδίκη, πυκασώμεθα, καὶ τὸν ἄκρατον
ἕλκωμεν, κύλικας μείζονας αἰρόμενοι.
βαιὸς ὁ χαιρόντων ἐστὶν βίος· εἶτα τὰ λοιπὰ
γῆρας κωλύσει, καὶ τὸ τέλος θάνατος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.14: Εὐρώπης τὸ φίλημα, καὶ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
Εὐρώπης τὸ φίλημα, καὶ ἢν ἄχρι χείλεος ἔλθῃ,
ἡδύ γε, κἂν ψαύσῃ μοῦνον ἄκρου στόματος·
ψαύει δʼ οὐκ ἄκροις τοῖς χείλεσιν, ἀλλʼ ἐρίσασα
τὸ στόμα τὴν ψυχὴν ἐξ ὀνύχων ἀνάγει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.15: ποῦ νῦν Πραξιτέλης; ποῦ
poems.author: Rufinus

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.18: μᾶλλον τῶν σοβαρῶν τὰς
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
μᾶλλον τῶν σοβαρῶν τὰς δουλίδας ἐκλεγόμεσθα,
οἱ μὴ τοῖς σπαταλοῖς κλέμμασι τερπόμενοι.
ταῖς μὲν χρὼς ἀπόδωδε μύρου, σοβαρόν τε φρύαγμα,
καὶ μέχρι † κινδύνου ἑσπομένη σύνοδος·
ταῖς δὲ χάρις καὶ χρὼς ἴδιος, καὶ λέκτρον ἑτοῖμον,
δώροις ἐκ σπατάλης οὐκ † ἀλεγιζόμενον.
μιμοῦμαι Πύρρον τὸν Ἀχιλλέος, ὃς προέκρινεν
Ἑρμιόνης ἀλόχου τὴν λάτριν Ἀνδρομάχην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.19: οὐκέτι παιδομανὴς ὡς πρίν
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
οὐκέτι παιδομανὴς ὡς πρίν ποτε, νῦν δὲ καλοῦμαι
θηλυμανής, καὶ νῦν δίσκος ἐμοὶ κρόταλον·
ἀντὶ δέ μοι παίδων ἀδόλου χροὸς ἤρεσε γύψου
χρώματα, καὶ φύκους ἄνθος ἐπεισόδιον.
βοσκήσει δελφῖνας ὁ δενδροκόμης Ἐρύμανθος,
καὶ πολιὸν πόντου κῦμα θοὰς ἐλάφους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.21: οὐκ ἔλεγον, Προδίκη, Γηράσκομεν
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
οὐκ ἔλεγον, Προδίκη, Γηράσκομεν ; οὐ προεφώνουν
ἥξουσιν ταχέως αἱ διαλυσίφιλοι ;
νῦν ῥυτίδες καὶ θρὶξ πολιὴ καὶ σῶμα ῥακῶδες,
καὶ στόμα τὰς προτέρας οὐκέτʼ ἔχον χάριτας.
μή τις σοι, μετέωρε, προσέρχεται, ἢ κολακεύων
λίσσεται; ὡς δὲ τάφον νῦν σε παρερχόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.22: σοί με λάτριν γλυκύδωρος
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
σοί με λάτριν γλυκύδωρος Ἔρως παρέδωκε, Βοῶπι,
ταῦρον ὑποζεύξας εἰς πόθον αὐτόμολον,
αὐτοθελῆ, πάνδουλον, ἑκούσιον, αὐτοκέλευστον,
αἰτήσοντα πικρὴν μήποτʼ ἐλευθερίην
ἄχρι, φίλη, πολιῆς καὶ γήραος· ὄμμα βάλοι δὲ
μήποτʼ ἐφʼ ἡμετέραις ἐλπίσι βασκανίη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.27: ποῦ σοι κεῖνα, Μέλισσα,
poems.author: Rufinus

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.28: νῦν μοι χαῖρε λέγεις,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
νῦν μοι χαῖρε λέγεις, ὅτε σου τὸ πρόσωπον ἀπῆλθεν
κεῖνο, τὸ τῆς λύγδου, βάσκανε, λειότερον·
νῦν μοι προσπαίζεις, ὅτε τὰς τρίχας ἠφάνικάς σου,
τὰς ἐπὶ τοῖς σοβαροῖς αὐχέσι πλαζομένας.
μηκέτι μοι, μετέωρε, προσέρχεο, μηδὲ συνάντα·
ἀντὶ ῥόδου γὰρ ἐγὼ τὴν βάτον οὐ δέχομαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.35: πυγὰς αὐτὸς ἔκρινα τριῶν
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
πυγὰς αὐτὸς ἔκρινα τριῶν εἵλοντο γὰρʼ αὐταὶ,
δείξασαι γυμνὴν ἀστεροπὴν μελέων.
καὶ ῥʼ ἡ μὲν τροχαλοῖς σφραγιζομένη γελασίνοις
λευκῇ ἀπὸ γλουτῶν ἤνθεεν εὐαφίῃ·
τῆς δὲ διαιρομένης φοινίσσετο χιονέη σάρξ,.
πορφυρέοιο ῥόδου μᾶλλον ἐρυθροτέρη·
ἡ δὲ γαληνιόωσα χαράσσετο κύματι κωφῷ,
αὐτομάτη τρυφερῷ χρωτὶ σαλευομένη.
εἰ ταύτας ὁ κριτὴς ὁ θεῶν ἐθεήσατο πυγάς,
οὐκέτʼ ἂν οὐδʼ ἐσιδεῖν ἤθελε τὰς προτέρας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.36: ἤρισαν ἀλλήλαις Ῥοδόπη, Μελίτη,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ἤρισαν ἀλλήλαις Ῥοδόπη, Μελίτη, Ῥοδόκλεια,
τῶν τρισσῶν τίς ἔχει κρείσσονα μηριόνην,
καί με κριτὴν εἵλοντο· καὶ ὡς θεαὶ αἱ περίβλεπτοι
ἔστησαν γυμναί, νέκταρι λειβόμεναι.
καὶ Ῥοδόπης μὲν ἔλαμπε μέσος μηρῶν Πολύφημος
οἷα ῥοδὼν πολίῳ σχιζόμενος ζεφύρῳ
τῆς δὲ Ῥοδοκλείης ὑάλῳ ἴσος, ὑγρομέτωπος,
οἷα καὶ ἐν νηῷ πρωτογλυφὲς ξόανον.
ἀλλὰ σαφῶς ἃ πέπονθε Πάρις διὰ τὴν κρίσιν εἰδὼς,
τὰς τρεῖς ἀθανάτας εὐθὺ συνεστεφάνουν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.37: Μήτʼ ἰσχνὴν λίην περιλάμβανε,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
Μήτʼ ἰσχνὴν λίην περιλάμβανε, μήτε παχεῖαν
τούτων δʼ ἀμφοτέρων τὴν μεσότητα θέλε.
τῇ μὲν γὰρ λείπει σαρκῶν χύσις, ἡ δὲ περισσὴν
κέκτηται· λεῖπον μὴ θέλε, μηδὲ πλέον·

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.41: τίς γυμνὴν οὕτω σε
poems.author: Rufinus

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.42: μισῶ τὴν ἀφελῆ, μισῶ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
μισῶ τὴν ἀφελῆ, μισῶ τὴν σώφρονα λίαν·
ἡ μὲν γὰρ βραδέως, ἡ δὲ θέλει ταχέως.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.43: ἐκβάλλει γυμνήν τις, ἐπὴν
poems.author: Rufinus

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.44: Λέμβιον, ἡ δʼ ἑτέρα
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
Λέμβιον, ἡ δʼ ἑτέρα Κερκούριον, αἱ δύʼ ἑταῖραι
αἰὲν ἐφορμοῦσιν τῷ Σαμίων λιμένι.
ἀλλά, νέοι, πανδημὶ τὰ λῃστρικὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης
φεύγεθʼ· ὁ συμμίξας καὶ καταδὺς πίεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.47: πολλάκις ἠρασάμην σε λαβὼν
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
πολλάκις ἠρασάμην σε λαβὼν ἐν νυκτί, Θάλεια,
πληρῶσαι θαλερῇ θυμὸν ἐρωμανίῃ·̓·
νῦν δʼ ὅτε μοι γυμνὴ γλυκεροῖς; μελέεσσι πέπλησαι,
ἔκλυτος ὑπναλέῳ γυῖα κέκμηκα κόπῳ.
θυμὲ τάλαν, τί πέπονθας; ἀνέγρεο, μηδʼ ἀπόκαμνε·
ζητήσεις ταύτην τὴν ὑπερευτυχίην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.48: ὄμματα μὲν χρύσεια, καὶ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ὄμματα μὲν χρύσεια, καὶ ὑαλόεσσα παρειή,
καὶ στόμα πορφυρέης τερπνότερον κάλυκος,
δειρὴ λυγδινέη, καὶ στήθεα μαρμαίροντα,
καὶ πόδες ἀργυρέης λευκότεροι Θέτιδος.
εἰ δέ τι καὶ πλοκαμῖσι διαστίλβουσιν ἄκανθαι,
τῆς λευκῆς καλάμης οὐδὲν ἐπιστρέφομαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.60: παρθένος ἀργυρόπεζος ἐλούετο, χρύσεα
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
παρθένος ἀργυρόπεζος ἐλούετο, χρύσεα μαζῶν
χρωτὶ γαλακτοπαγεῖ μῆλα διαινομένη·
πυγαὶ δʼ ἀλλήλαις περιηγέες εἱλίσσοντο,
ὕδατος ὑγροτέρῳ χρωτὶ σαλευόμεναι. ˘ ˘
τὸν δʼ ὑπεροιδαίνοντα κατέσκεπε πεπταμένη χεὶρ
οὐχ ὅλον Εὐρώταν, ἀλλʼ ὅσον ἠδύνατο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.61: τῇ κυανοβλεφάρῳ παίζων κόνδακα
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
τῇ κυανοβλεφάρῳ παίζων κόνδακα Φιλίππῃ,
ἐξ αὐτῆς κραδίης ἡδὺ γελᾶν ἐπόουν· ¯
“δώδεκά σοι βέβληκα, καὶ αὔριον ἄλλα βαλῶ σοι,
ἢ πλέον, ἠὲ πάλιν δώδεκʼ ἐπιστάμενος.”
εἶτα κελευομένη † ἦλθεν γελάσας δὲ πρὸς αὐτήν

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.62: οὔπω σου τὸ καλὸν
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
οὔπω σου τὸ καλὸν χρόνος ἔσβεσεν, ἀλλʼ ἔτι πολλὰ
λείψανα τῆς προτέρης σῴζεται ἡλικίης, ˘ ˘
καὶ χάριτες μίμνουσιν ἀγήραοι, οὐδὲ τὸ κάλλος
τῶν ἱλαρῶν μήλων ἢ ῥόδου ἐξέφυγεν.
ὦ πόσσους κατέφλεξε τὸ πρὶν θεοείκελον ἄνθος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.66: εὐκαίρως μονάσασαν ἰδὼν Προδίκην
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
εὐκαίρως μονάσασαν ἰδὼν Προδίκην ἱκέτευον,
καὶ τῶν ἀμβροσίων ἁψάμενος γονάτων,
σῶσον, ἔφην, “ἄνθρωπον ἀπολλύμενον παρὰ μικρόν
καὶ φεῦγον ζωῆς πνεῦμα σύ μοι χάρισαι.”
ταῦτα λέγοντος ἔκλαυσεν ἀποψήσασα δὲ δάκρυ,
ταῖς τρυφεραῖς ἡμᾶς χερσὶν ὑπεξέβαλεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.69: Παλλὰς ἐσαθρήσασα καὶ Ἥρη
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
Παλλὰς ἐσαθρήσασα καὶ Ἥρη χρυσοπέδιλος
Μαιονίδʼ, ἐκ κραδίης ἴαχον ἀμφότεραι·
“οὐκέτι γυμνούμεσθα· κρίσις μία ποιμένος ἀρκεῖ·
οὐ καλὸν ἡττᾶσθαι δὶς περὶ καλλοσύνης.”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.70: κάλλος ἔχεις Κύπριδος;, Πειθοῦς
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
κάλλος ἔχεις Κύπριδος;, Πειθοῦς στόμα, σῶμα καὶ ἀκμὴν
εἰαρινῶν Ὡρῶν, φθέγμα δὲ Καλλιόπης,
νοῦν καὶ σωφροσύνην Θέμιδος, καὶ χεῖρας Ἀθήνης·
σὺν σοὶ δʼ αἱ Χάριτες τέσσαρές εἰσι, Φίλη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.73: δαίμονες, οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
δαίμονες, οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι λούεται ἡ Κυθέρεια,
χερσὶ καταυχενίους λυσαμένη πλοκάμους.
ἱλήκοις, δέσποινα, καὶ ὄμμασιν ἡμετέροισι
μήποτε μηνίσῃς, θεῖον ἰδοῦσι τύπον.
νῦν ἔγνων Ῥοδόκλεια, καὶ οὐ Κύπρις. εἶτα τὸ κάλλος
τοῦτο πόθεν; σύ, δοκῶ, τὴν θεὸν ἐκδέδυκας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.74: πέμπω σοι, Ῥοδόκλεια, τόδε
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
πέμπω σοι, Ῥοδόκλεια, τόδε στέφος, ἄνθεσι καλοῖς
αὐτὸς ὑφʼ ἡμετέραις πλεξάμενος παλάμαις.
ἔστι κρίνον, ῥοδέη τε κάλυξ, νοτερὴ τʼ ἀνεμώνη,
καὶ νάρκισσος ὑγρός, καὶ κυαναυγὲς ἴον.
ταῦτα στεψαμένη, λῆξον μεγάλαυχος ἐοῦσα·
ἀνθεῖς καὶ λήγεις καὶ σὺ καὶ ὁ στέφανος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.75: γείτονα παρθένον εἶχον Ἀμυμώνην,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
γείτονα παρθένον εἶχον Ἀμυμώνην, Ἀφροδίτη,
ἥ μου τὴν ψυχὴν ἔφλεγεν οὐκ ὀλίγον.
αὕτη μοι προσέπαιξε, καί, εἴ ποτε καιρός, ἐτόλμων
ἠρυθρία. τί πλέον; τὸν πόνον ᾐσθάνετο·
ἤνυσα πολλὰ καμών. παρακήκοα νῦν ὅτι τίκτει·
ὥστε τί ποιοῦμεν; φεύγομεν ἢ μένομεν;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.76: αὕτη πρόσθεν ἔην ἐρατόχροος,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
αὕτη πρόσθεν ἔην ἐρατόχροος, εἰαρόμασθος,
εὔσφυρος, εὐμήκης, εὔοφρυς, εὐπλόκαμος·
ἠλλάχθη δὲ χρόνῳ καὶ γήραϊ καὶ πολιαῖσι,
καὶ νῦν τῶν προτέρων οὐδʼ ὄναρ οὐδὲν ἔχει,
ἀλλοτρίας δὲ τρίχας, καὶ ῥυσῶδες τὸ πρόσωπον,
οἷον γηράσας οὐδὲ πίθηκος ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.77: εἰ τοίην χάριν εἶχε
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
εἰ τοίην χάριν εἶχε γυνὴ μετὰ Κύπριδος εὐνήν,
οὐκ ἄν τοι κόρον ἔσχεν ἀνὴρ ἀλόχοισιν ὁμιλῶν.
πᾶσαι γὰρ μετὰ κύπριν ἀτερπέες εἰσὶ γυναῖκες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.87: ἀρνεῖται τὸν ἔρωτα Μελισσιάς,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ἀρνεῖται τὸν ἔρωτα Μελισσιάς, ἀλλὰ τὸ σῶμα
κέκραγʼ ὡς βελέων δεξάμενον φαρέτρην,
καὶ βάσις ἀστατέουσα, καὶ ἄστατος ἄσθματος ὁρμή,
καὶ κοῖλαι βλεφάρων ἰοτυπεῖς βάσιες.
ἀλλά, Πόθοι, πρὸς μητρὸς ἐϋστεφάνου Κυθερείης,
φλέξατε τὴν ἀπιθῆ, μέχρις ἐρεῖ Φλέγομαι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.88: εἰ δυσὶν οὐκ ἴσχυσας
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
εἰ δυσὶν οὐκ ἴσχυσας ἴσην φλόγα, πυρφόρε, καῦσαι,
τὴν ἑνὶ καιομένην ἢ σβέσον ἢ μετάθες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.92: ὑψοῦται Ῥοδόπη τῷ κάλλεϊ·
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ὑψοῦται Ῥοδόπη τῷ κάλλεϊ· κἤν ποτε “χαῖρε”
εἴπω, ταῖς σοβαραῖς ὀφρύσιν ἠσπάσατο.
ἤν ποτε καὶ στεφάνους προθύρων ὕπερ ἐκκρεμάσωμαι,
ὀργισθεῖσα πατεῖ τοῖς σοβαροῖς ἴχνεσιν.
ὦ ῥυτίδες, καὶ γῆρας ἀνηλεές, ἔλθετε θᾶσσον,
σπεύσατε· κἂν ὑμεῖς πείσατε τὴν Ῥοδόπην,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.93: ὥπλισμαι πρὸς ;ἔρωτα περὶ
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ὥπλισμαι πρὸς ;ἔρωτα περὶ στέρνοισι λογισμόν,
οὐδέ με νικήσει, μοῦνος ἐὼν πρὸς ἕνα·
θνατὸς δʼ ἀθανάτῳ συστήσομαι·
ἢν δὲ βοηθὸν
Βάκχον ἔχῃ, τί μόνος πρὸς δύʼ ἐγὼ δύναμαι;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.94: ὄμματʼ ἔχεις Ἥρης, Μελίτη,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
ὄμματʼ ἔχεις Ἥρης, Μελίτη, τὰς χεῖρας Ἀθήνης,
τοὺς μαζοὺς Παφίης, τὰ σφυρὰ τῆς Θέτιδος.
εὐδαίμων ὁ βλέπων σε· ;τρισόλβιος ὅστις ἀκούει·
ἡμίθεος δʼ ὁ φιλῶν ἀθάνατος δʼ ὁ γαμῶν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.97: εἰ μὲν ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέροισιν,
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
εἰ μὲν ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέροισιν, Ἔρως, ἴσα τόξα τιταίνεις,
εἶ θεός· εἰ δὲ ῥέπεις πρὸς μέρος, οὐ θεὸς εἶ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.103: μέχρι τίνος, Προδίκη, παρακλαύσομαι;
poems.author: Rufinus
poems.text:
μέχρι τίνος, Προδίκη, παρακλαύσομαι; ἄχρι τίνος σε
γουνάσομαι, στερεή, μηδὲν ἀκουόμενος;
ἤδη καὶ λευκαί σοι ἐπισκιρτῶσιν ἔθειραι,
καὶ τάχα μοι δώσεις ὡς Ἑκάβη Πριάμῳ.
